title: Your teachers
hook: the people who taught you anything true

segments.voice: Yesterday: unknown teachers, the grandmothers, chanters and village monks the books let go. Your line: no one wrote them down.

A note in red pen in the margin of an old school essay: good, now say what you mean. A coach's voice from the sideline, repeating the same two words all season. An aunt in a kitchen, measuring salt by the look of it, not the spoon. Some teachers have titles. Some have none: a coworker, a kid down the street, a stranger on a long bus ride who told the truth when a polite lie would have been easier. Today turns the lamp toward the teachers in a life like yours.

Today's text is the Buddha's advice to a young householder named Sigala. As the story goes, Sigala's dying father told him to honor the directions, so each morning Sigala bows to the east, south, west, north, the sky and the earth. The Buddha gives the old custom a new meaning. The directions, he says, are the people in your life: parents, teachers, a spouse and children, friends, workers, and religious teachers. Honor them by how you treat them. The teachers are the south. A student looks after a teacher by rising to greet them, attending on them, wanting to learn, listening closely. Then the text turns around: a teacher owes the student good training, makes sure they've really grasped what was taught, and speaks well of them to friends. So a teacher isn't a vending machine for facts. A teacher keeps an eye on you, checks you understood, and is proud of you in public. The same discourse describes a true friend who sounds a lot like a teacher: the friend who gives good counsel. That friend keeps you from wrong, encourages you in what is good, tells you what you hadn't heard before, and shows you the way to heaven. No robe is mentioned. Learning here happens in households and friendships, not only temples. A teacher might be the monk at the local vihara. It might be the friend who drove you to the hospital, or the boss who corrected you without shaming you. The text doesn't call every friend a teacher. It describes what the good ones do.
screen: `STUDENT AND TEACHER LOOK AFTER EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Let three people come to mind who taught you something true; not the most important three, just three. For each, find the single thing they taught you in a few plain words, like she taught me to finish what I start, and hold it for a few breaths before moving on. If someone difficult shows up on the list, that's allowed; hard teachers count too.
Your teachers. The people who taught you anything true, with or without a title. In the advice to Sigala, they're a direction worth bowing to.
Your line: proud of you in public. That's what the good ones do. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists in many places honor teachers with bows, offerings and gratitude ceremonies, and the advice to Sigala is taught in some communities as a guide to everyday relationships, teachers among them.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a young man is bowing to the directions each morning because his dying father told him to. what do you do?
options: tell him the custom is useless.
show him the directions stand for the people in his life.
walk past; it's his family's business.
fork.reveal: the Buddha keeps the bow and gives it meaning: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers and religious teachers, each honored by how he treats them.

original.note: Pali disa: a direction; in the advice to Sigala, the people a person honors.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher is someone at the front of a classroom.
what it means: in the advice to Sigala, teachers are a direction you honor, and a good one checks you understood and speaks well of you.
what a scholar hears: the six directions of DN 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), teachers as the south, the reciprocal duties of pupil and teacher, and the friend who counsels (atthakkhāyī).
recall: a laywoman who practiced through grief

chat.says: Does a Buddhist teacher have to be a monk in a robe?
options: No; in the advice to Sigala, a friend who gives good counsel teaches, no robe needed.
Yes, only ordained monks may ever be called someone's teacher.
No, and anyone who gives you advice at all counts as a teacher, good or bad.
chat.meaning: In the advice to Sigala, the friend who gives good counsel keeps you from wrong and tells you what you hadn't heard. No robe is mentioned.

notes: Editor: teach, hook, word, games and original rewritten. The draft rebuilt day 1023 (SN 45.2 'half the holy life', kalyanamitta gloss, identical myth and fork) and opened like day 1025's hook ('who taught you to ride a bike'); the day now rests on DN 31 alone: Sigala's directions, teachers as the south, reciprocal duties, and the counseling friend (keeps from wrong, encourages good, tells what was unheard, shows the way to heaven). SN 45.2 notes below no longer apply. Confirm the DN 31 summary.
SN 45.2 paraphrased: Ananda proposes good friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha says it is the whole. Confirm wording 'can be expected to develop the path' as a fair summary.
Ananda described as the Buddha's attendant and cousin; tradition holds he was a cousin. Confirm or cut 'and cousin'.
Gloss kalyāṇa = good/lovely, mitta = friend is a standard reading of the compound, not an etymology claim. Confirm.
DN 31 duties of pupil and teacher summarized selectively (the text lists more on each side); the script deliberately gives no count. Confirm the selection is fair.
'In these texts, learning the path happens between people' is an interpretive summary of the two texts; soften if needed.
